newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-SPD accuses Bonn govt of borrowing blowout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SPD accuses Bonn govt of borrowing blowout.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrat (SPD) opposition on Friday accused the Bonn government of blowing its borrowing targets, but the Finance Ministry said the SPD was looking at the wrong numbers.

Social Democrat finance spokesman Karl Diller said that in the first quarter Chancellor Helmut Kohl's federal government had used up 40 billion marks ($23.3 billion) out of the 53.4 billion marks it has allowed for its budget deficit for the whole of 1997.
"This is a first in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany," Diller said in a statement. "Kohl's chaos cabinet will exceed the year's budget deficit in a few weeks."
But a Finance Ministry spokesman replied that Diller's figure was in fact the federal government's first quarter cash shortfall, a number reported this week by the Bundesbank.
It was not possible to use the volatile cash deficit from the first few months of the year as a basis for extrapolating the budget deficit for the whole year, he said.
Net new borrowing -- a figure offering a better guide to how the budget deficit will turn out -- was just 14.3 billion marks in the first quarter, the spokesman added.
Germany's federal deficit forms the largest chunk of its total public sector deficit, which Finance Minister Theo Waigel intends to cut to 105 billion marks this year.

That sum is equivalent to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, and just inside the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty which Waigel says he wants to hit exactly to qualify for European monetary union in 1999.

Payments into the EU budget had been made early, while petrol tax revenues in the new year had been below past levels due to changes in payment dates, the spokesman said. "This will have no impact on the full-year result."

The Bundesbank, in its April report published this week, said the federal cash deficit in the first three months was 39.7 billion marks, almost double the 20.5 billion marks in the same period a year earlier.
But the central bank added: "It should be pointed out that the results of the cash accounts -- above all in the early months of the year -- are not a reliable indicator for the budget deficit."
The SPD's Diller said federal spending in the first quarter exceeded budget targets by 7.3 percent, while tax revenues fell 9.9 percent short of target.
He repeated his argument that tax revenue estimates for 1997, due next month, would have to be revised down 20 billion marks from the previous six-monthly forecast last November.

Waigel earlier this week rejected that figure, saying that he had already taken into account a shortfall of eight billion marks in his budget planning and that, if exceeded, the figure would only have to be revised slightly upwards.
Parliament's finance committee will discuss the budget with Waigel next Wednesday -- the day more talks between the coalition and SPD on planned tax reforms have also been set.
Diller said the SPD at the committee meeting would press its motion calling for a supplementary budget, something that Kohl's ruling coalition has rejected so far.

He added that if the government took no action, it risked contravening budget law and the constitution, which state that the deficit cannot exceed government investment spending, budgeted at 59.6 billion marks this year. ($ = 1.718 German Marks)
